passage: Every evening at seven, after the school bell had stopped ringing in his head, Akash sat on the steps of his rented room in Almora with a small notebook and a steel cup of tea. His landlady, Rukmini aunty, watched from her kitchen window the first few days, curious. Akash wrote for exactly fifteen minutes. The inspection next month. His mother's knees. Whether the Class 8 students liked him. The leaking tap. Then he took a red pen and put a star next to anything he could do something about. The tap got a star. So did the inspection. He chose one, the tap, and knocked on Rukmini aunty's door. "Can I call the plumber tomorrow?" "Of course, beta." The rest he left in the notebook. When they came back at night, he told himself, "Seven o'clock tomorrow." By the second week he was sleeping through.

qa.q: What did Akash use to mark the worries he could act on?
qa.a: A red pen, with a star.

qa.q: How did Akash seem to feel after a couple of weeks of the routine?
qa.a: He seemed calmer and more settled, sleeping through instead of spinning at night.

qa.q: What could Akash do with the inspection worry, now that it has a star?
qa.a: He could pick one small step, like listing what the inspector checks, and do it in the next day's action slot.

qa.q: How might Rukmini aunty see Akash's evening notebook?
qa.a: Rukmini aunty seems curious at first, then helpful when he asks about the plumber, perhaps warmly amused by the ritual.

grounding: It shows an adult who writes worries in a fifteen-minute window, marks the solvable ones, acts on one and leaves the rest for the next window.

passage: In the break room of the engineering firm in Toronto, Abebe set a timer on his phone: fifteen minutes. His colleague Jin raised an eyebrow. "Meditation?" "Worry time." He wrote on a sheet: visa renewal, project deadline, mother's surgery back home, the presentation, whether his English sounded stiff in meetings. Then he drew a line down the middle. Solvable on one side, not solvable on the other. The visa renewal: solvable, email the HR office. The surgery: not in his hands; he could call his mother, but he couldn't operate. He picked the visa email and sent it right there. When the timer rang, he folded the sheet. "The rest can wait till tomorrow's fifteen," he said. Jin laughed. "You're weirdly calm." Abebe smiled. "Weirdly calm is new for me. Three months ago I was up every night."

qa.q: What did Abebe write on the solvable side?
qa.a: The visa renewal.

qa.q: How does Abebe feel compared with three months ago?
qa.a: He feels calmer, even 'weirdly calm', compared with three months ago, when worries kept him up every night.

qa.q: What made Abebe's approach work?
qa.a: Splitting worries into solvable and not solvable, acting on one right away, and giving the rest a set time kept planning useful and stopped endless spinning.

qa.q: How does Jin see Abebe's worry time?
qa.a: Jin is curious and a bit amused, noticing Abebe's calm and maybe tempted to try it.

grounding: It shows an adult using a fifteen-minute worry window to separate solvable worries from the rest, acting on one and letting the others wait.

passage: Baljeet, you cried when you lost the cricket match today? Come, sit. Let me tell you about the kho-kho final when I was a girl of nine, in our school in Amritsar. We lost by one point, and it was my fault. I was caught at the last second. I ran behind the school wall and cried so hard I couldn't breathe. My father found me. He didn't say, "Stop crying." He sat on the ground in his good trousers and held me. "You're sad. That's okay. I'm here." I cried until it was finished. Then he wiped my face and said, "Shall we practise that dodge tomorrow?" I nodded. The next morning we practised in the courtyard. The next year, we won. Shalini's secret, beta: it's easier to try again when someone holds you first.

qa.q: Where did young Shalini run to cry?
qa.a: Behind the school wall.

qa.q: How did young Shalini feel after her father held her?
qa.a: Shalini felt safe enough to cry until the sadness finished, then calm and willing to try again.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Shalini bounce back?
qa.a: Her father chose to hold her and name her sadness instead of telling her to stop crying, then offered practice together the next day.

qa.q: How might Shalini's father have felt sitting on the ground in his good trousers?
qa.a: He probably felt tender and sad for her, caring more about comforting her than about his clothes.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a child, being comforted after losing a game made it safe to feel sad and then try again.

passage: The inter-school chess tournament in Chennai was held in a crowded hall with fans that barely worked. Karthik, eight, lost his second game in twelve moves. He walked out to the corridor, face hot, and started crying behind a pillar. His mother Disha was supposed to be there, but she was stuck in traffic. A volunteer sat near him. Twenty minutes later Disha rushed in, breathless, and found him. She knelt and hugged him. "You lost. That hurts." Karthik sobbed into her shoulder. She waited, rubbing his back. When he was calm, she gave him a banana and said, "Round three starts in ten minutes. Do you want to play?" He sniffed. "What if I lose again?" "Then I'll hug you again." Karthik laughed a little, wiped his nose, and walked back to the board.

qa.q: How many moves did Karthik's second game last?
qa.a: Twelve moves.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel after his mother's hug?
qa.a: Karthik felt comforted and calm enough to laugh a little, safe to try again because his mother would be there either way.

qa.q: What did Disha's response get right?
qa.a: She named his hurt, let him cry without rushing, and then offered the next round with the promise of support, not pressure.

qa.q: How might the volunteer have felt waiting near Karthik?
qa.a: The volunteer may have felt concerned and relieved when his mother finally arrived.

grounding: It shows a child who cries after losing a game, is comforted by his mother, and then tries again, with warmth making hard feelings safe.

passage: On the Sunday after Diwali, Chetan, ten, played carrom with the older boys in the building in Pune. He lost every game. After the last one, he threw the striker and ran upstairs. Rehana aunty from next door, who had watched, followed him. She found him on the stairs, crying into his knees. She sat beside him. "Losing three times in a row. That's hard." He nodded without looking up. She didn't tell him to stop. She just stayed. After a while he said, "They're all better than me." "They're older. They've played longer. You got two coins on the first shot, I saw." He looked up. "You saw that?" "I did. Want to practise that shot with me tomorrow?" Chetan wiped his face. The next evening he was back at the board, lips pressed together, aiming carefully.

qa.q: How many games did Chetan lose?
qa.a: He lost every game, three in a row.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel when Rehana aunty mentioned the two coins?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a bit comforted that she had noticed something he did well, which made trying again feel possible.

qa.q: How did Rehana aunty help Chetan bounce back?
qa.a: She sat with him, named his hurt, stayed quietly, pointed out a real strength, and offered to practise together.

qa.q: How might the older boys see Chetan coming back the next evening?
qa.a: They might be surprised and impressed that he returned after losing every game.

grounding: It shows a child who cries after losing a game, is comforted by a warm neighbour, and then tries again.

passage:
Thursday

The school band list went up today. My name wasn't there. Rafiq's was.

At lunch Rafiq asked, "You okay?" and I was going to say "fine", like always. But I'm tired of "fine". So I said, "Honestly? I'm disappointed. And embarrassed, because I told everyone I'd get in."

He just nodded and said, "Yeah, that makes sense." And somehow that was enough. I didn't cry. By the last period I was actually laughing at his terrible drum jokes.

Last year when I didn't make the quiz team, I said "fine" for a whole week and felt awful the entire time. Today I said the real words and it was over by afternoon.

Weird. Saying it made it smaller.

— Uma

qa.q: Whose name was on the band list?
qa.a: Rafiq's.

qa.q: How did Uma feel after saying 'disappointed' and 'embarrassed' out loud?
qa.a: Uma felt lighter and calmer, surprised that naming the feelings made them smaller, and was laughing by the last period.

qa.q: Why did naming the feelings help Uma more than saying 'fine'?
qa.a: Putting words to the disappointment and embarrassment let Uma feel understood and settle quickly, while 'fine' last year kept the feelings stuck for a week.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel when Uma is honest with him?
qa.a: Rafiq may feel trusted and a bit relieved to know what's really going on, so he can simply be there.

grounding: It shows a teenager who says they are disappointed and embarrassed instead of fine, and gets through the moment more quickly.

passage: In Navsari, the inter-school kabaddi final was played during the Navratri holidays, under strings of lights left from the garba nights. Disha, fifteen, was dropped from the starting seven at the last minute. She sat on the bench, jaw tight. At the break, coach Zubin sir came over. "All right?" She almost said fine. Instead she said, quietly, "No, sir. I'm disappointed. And a bit embarrassed. My parents came to watch." Zubin sir sat down next to her. "That's fair. Thank you for telling me." He explained why he'd chosen a defender tonight. It still stung, but the knot in her stomach loosened. In the second half, when he sent her in for the last five minutes, she was ready. She made one clean tackle. Her father cheered from the stands.

qa.q: When was the kabaddi final played?
qa.a: During the Navratri holidays.

qa.q: How did Disha feel after telling Zubin sir she was disappointed and embarrassed?
qa.a: It still stung, but she felt the knot in her stomach loosen, calmer and ready when sent in.

qa.q: Why did naming her feelings help Disha get back in the game?
qa.a: Saying the real feelings let Zubin sir respond and explain, which settled her mind instead of leaving her stewing on the bench.

qa.q: How might Zubin sir see Disha's honesty?
qa.a: Zubin sir seems to appreciate it, thanking her and explaining his decision, which builds trust.

grounding: It shows a teenager who names her disappointment and embarrassment instead of saying fine, and settles quickly enough to play well.

passage:
Dear Yogesh bhaiya,

I've been trying to write this for a week. Since we moved to Bhopal, I haven't really been okay. I eat lunch alone. I don't sleep well. Some days I don't want to go to school at all. I didn't tell Mummy because she's busy with the new job and I didn't want to add to it.

But you said once, when I was small, "If anything's heavy, tell me." So I'm telling you.

I'm not in danger or anything. I just feel really alone. Can we talk on Sunday? And maybe you can help me figure out how to tell Mummy too. I think I should.

Vaibhav

passage: Preeti, you asked how I got through Class 10 when things at home were bad. Okay. My parents were separating, the house was loud every night, and I stopped doing homework. I didn't tell anyone. I thought if I just kept quiet, it'd pass. Then my marks fell, and I felt worse. One day Anjali ma'am, our English teacher, asked me to stay after class. She said, "Payal, you've been very quiet. Is something going on?" And I don't know why, but I just told her. Everything. I cried in the staff room. She listened, then she took me to the school counsellor that same afternoon. The counsellor called my mother, gently. Things at home didn't get fixed right away. But I wasn't alone with it anymore. That's the part that saved me. Telling someone. So, Preeti, if you're carrying something, tell me. That's all.

qa.q: Which teacher asked Payal to stay after class?

qa.a: Payal felt alone and worse as the marks fell, keeping everything quiet in the hope it would pass.

qa.q: What did Anjali ma'am do that helped?

qa.q: How might Preeti feel hearing Payal's story?

passage: When the results came, I'd failed the corporate law paper. I sat in the college library and let myself feel it. I was disappointed. Properly disappointed; I'd wanted a first class. I didn't tell myself it didn't matter. It did. After a while, I asked a different question: what does this tell me about how I prepared? I went back through my notes. I had read the cases, but never practised writing answers under time. My friend Lalit had done three mock papers. I had done none. That wasn't about my brain. It was about my method. So I signed up for the re-exam and asked Lalit if we could do timed papers together on Saturdays. I still felt the sting. But I also felt I had somewhere to go. I'm Tanuja, and failing that paper taught me more than passing some others.

qa.q: How many mock papers had Lalit done?
qa.a: Three mock papers.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel after failing, and what did Tanuja do with that feeling?
qa.a: Tanuja felt properly disappointed and let that be real, then turned it into a question about how the preparation went.

qa.q: What did Tanuja's reframe open up?
qa.a: Seeing the problem as method, not brain, led to the re-exam sign-up and Saturday timed papers with Lalit.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel being asked to study together?
qa.a: Lalit might feel pleased and trusted, happy to help a friend who is taking the setback seriously.

grounding: It shows a student who failed a paper, acknowledges the disappointment honestly, then asks what it says about preparation, which opens options.

passage:
Tutor's note, Monday

Jomon came to office hours after failing the mid-term in microeconomics. He didn't pretend it was fine. He said, "I'm really disappointed. I thought I understood it." I told him that disappointment made sense.

Then he surprised me. He said, "But I want to know what it tells me about how I studied." We went through the paper together. His concepts were fine. He lost marks on the graphs, every time, because he had only read the textbook and never drawn them himself.

He left with a plan: draw every graph by hand this week and bring five to me on Friday. He looked lighter going out than coming in, though he said the fail still stung.

— Uma

qa.q: What subject did Jomon fail?
qa.a: The mid-term in microeconomics.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel coming in, and how did that change?
qa.a: He came in really disappointed, admitting it honestly, and left looking lighter with a plan, though still stung.

qa.q: What did Jomon's question about how he studied reveal?
qa.a: It showed his concepts were fine but his method was missing hand-drawn graphs, which gave him a clear next step.

qa.q: How might Uma see Jomon's approach?
qa.a: Uma seems pleasantly surprised and impressed that Jomon moved from honest disappointment to curiosity about his preparation.

grounding: It shows, through a tutor's note, a student who admits disappointment after failing, then asks what it reveals about preparation, which keeps honesty and opens options.

passage:
Tuesday night

Failed the statistics paper. 34. Need 40.

I'm not going to pretend I'm okay. I'm disappointed. I cried in the bathroom at college. Deepak saw my face and just handed me a samosa, which honestly helped.

Tonight I made myself look at the paper. Not to punish myself. To ask: what does this tell me? I got the theory questions right. I lost all the marks on the calculations, because I was rushing and skipped steps. In the last two weeks I did no practice sums. Just reading.

So it's not that I'm bad at stats. It's that I prepared for the wrong kind of exam.

Plan: ten practice sums a day until the re-exam. Deepak said he'd check them.

Still sad. But not stuck.

Sangeeta

qa.q: What mark did Sangeeta get in statistics?
qa.a: 34. Need 40.

qa.q: How is Sangeeta feeling on Tuesday night?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels disappointed and sad, not pretending otherwise, but also 'not stuck' after finding a reason and a plan.

qa.q: Why does Sangeeta's question 'what does this tell me?' help?
qa.a: It turns the failure into information about preparation, showing that practice sums, not more reading, were needed, which opens a clear plan.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel being asked to check the sums?
qa.a: Deepak might feel glad to help and trusted, having already comforted Sangeeta with a samosa.

grounding: It shows a student who failed a paper, acknowledges disappointment, then asks what it reveals about preparation, keeping honesty while opening options.

passage: The final exams at the college in Chikmagalur were two weeks away, and Farida's mind was racing. She couldn't focus and didn't feel like eating. But she remembered what her roommate Lavanya had said last semester: "When your head's a mess, look after your body first." So she kept three things steady. Lights off at eleven, even if she hadn't finished. Breakfast in the mess, even if it was only idli and tea. A walk up the coffee estate road every evening, thirty minutes, even on days she didn't want to. Some days she walked slowly, dragging her feet. But she went. By the second week, her thoughts felt less jumbled. She wasn't cheerful. But she was coping. "And if it gets really bad," Lavanya reminded her, "the college counsellor's right there." Farida nodded. "I know. I'll go if it does."

qa.q: What three things did Farida keep steady?
qa.a: Lights off at eleven, breakfast in the mess, and a walk up the coffee estate road every evening.

qa.q: How did Farida feel during the two weeks, and what changed?
qa.a: She felt stressed and scattered at first, with no appetite, but by the second week her thoughts felt less jumbled and she was coping.

qa.q: Why did keeping body basics steady help Farida?
qa.a: Steady sleep, meals and walks supported her mind even when motivation was low, and she knew the counsellor was there if it got severe.

qa.q: How does Lavanya seem to support Farida?
qa.a: Lavanya offers practical advice and reminds her of the counsellor, showing she cares without pushing.

grounding: It shows a young adult under stress who keeps sleep, meals and walks steady despite low motivation, with a counsellor available if distress gets severe.

passage: Diego had been job hunting in Copenhagen for three months. Every rejection email made his stomach drop. Some mornings he didn't want to get out of bed. His flatmate Lars suggested a simple rule: whatever happens, keep the basics. So Diego set an alarm for eight and got up with it, even when he felt heavy. He ate breakfast at the table, not in bed. At four each afternoon he cycled along the canal for half an hour, rain or not. He didn't feel motivated. He just did it. Some days it barely helped. But the days when he skipped were worse. After a month, Lars noticed Diego humming while cooking. "Better?" "A bit. Still stressed." "If it gets really bad, see a doctor, okay?" Diego nodded. "I've already booked a check-up. Just in case."

qa.q: How did Diego feel during the job hunt, and how did the routine affect it?
qa.a: He felt stressed and heavy, his stomach dropping at rejections; the routine didn't remove it but made days less bad, and after a month he felt a bit better.

qa.q: Why was booking a check-up a wise step alongside the routine?
qa.a: Body basics support coping, but a doctor can help if the stress becomes severe or lasting.

grounding: It shows a young adult under stress who keeps sleep, meals and exercise steady even when motivation is low, with a doctor as a step if distress lasts.

passage: Mid-semester in the university hostel in Aligarh, the corridor smelled of instant noodles at two in the morning. Farida's assignments had piled up, and her sleep had gone. passage: Losing the job came on a Tuesday, in a ten-minute video call. The whole team was let go. For two days, I couldn't think. Everything felt huge at once: rent, my parents asking questions, whether I'd ever work again. On Thursday evening Kavitha, my wife, sat down with me and a notebook. "Let's just list it. All of it." We wrote: update CV, tell my parents, call three people I used to work with, check the final salary letter, look at two job sites. Then she said, "Pick one. Only one for tomorrow." I picked updating the CV. On Friday I did just that, nothing else. It took three hours. When I saved the file, I felt something I hadn't felt all week: that I could do something. Chinmay, a man with a list. The list is still long, but I keep ticking.

qa.a: Breaking the huge threat into a list and choosing one step made it manageable and gave him proof that action was possible.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel watching Chinmay tick off tasks?
qa.a: Kavitha likely feels relieved and affectionate, glad her husband is finding his feet again.

passage:
Career centre note, alumni support, Wednesday

Deepak came in two weeks after his company closed. He was shaking a little and said, "I don't even know where to start. Everything is falling down." He had not slept well.

I asked him to write down everything on his mind, without sorting. The list had fourteen items. Then we sorted: things he could do this week, and things for later. This week: update CV, email two former managers, tell his sister. He chose the CV as the first step.

He came back today with a finished CV. He said he'd also emailed one manager, who replied kindly. He still looked tired, but he sat up straighter and said, "It feels less like a wall now."

Next session Friday: interview practice.

— Mehak

qa.q: How many items were on Deepak's list?
qa.a: Fourteen items.

qa.q: How did Deepak seem to feel coming back with the finished CV?
qa.a: He seemed steadier and more hopeful, sitting up straighter, saying it felt less like a wall, though still tired.

qa.q: What did Mehak's sorting of the list achieve?
qa.a: It split a huge threat into this-week steps and later ones, so Deepak could start with one task and regain a sense of control.

qa.q: How might the former manager's kind reply have affected Deepak?

passage:
Friday

The startup shut down today. They told us at lunch. Pankaj came home early from his office and found me on the balcony, just staring. He made tea and sat with me. He didn't say much. That helped.

Tonight I couldn't sleep, so I got up and wrote a list:
1. Update portfolio.
2. Message five people from my old design school.
3. Tell Mamma before she hears from someone else.
4. Read the exit letter properly.
5. Rest this weekend.

It looked so much smaller on paper than in my head.

I'm starting with number 3 tomorrow, because it's the one that's sitting on my chest.

I'm scared. But I have a first step, and Pankaj put a star next to number 5.

Maria

qa.q: What is number 3 on Maria's list?
qa.a: Tell Mamma before she hears from someone else.

qa.q: How does Maria feel after writing the list?
qa.a: Maria still feels scared but calmer, finding the list looks much smaller on paper than in the head.

qa.q: Why does Maria choose number 3 first?
qa.a: It's the task weighing most, so doing it first can ease the heaviest pressure and start a sense of control.

qa.q: How does Pankaj show he cares?
qa.a: Pankaj makes tea, sits quietly with Maria, and stars the 'rest' item, gently showing affection and support.

grounding: It shows an adult facing job loss who writes a list of tasks and picks the first, which makes the threat feel more manageable.

passage:
Sunday

It's been four months since Papa died. The house is too quiet in the mornings.

Today I lit the lamp in front of his photo, the way Mummy does. At first I only did it because she asked. But now I like it. Ten quiet seconds where I talk to him in my head. It doesn't make it better. But it gives the missing a place to go.

Rekha came in the afternoon and we went to the old-age home where Papa used to volunteer on Sundays. I read the newspaper to Mr Fernandes, like Papa did. He said, "Your father had a funny voice for the headlines." I laughed, then cried a little. Mr Fernandes held my hand.

It still hurts. But on the way home I felt like Papa was a bit closer.

Sudha

qa.q: How long has it been since Sudha's father died?
qa.a: Four months.

qa.q: What does lighting the lamp seem to give Sudha?
qa.a: It gives the missing a place to go, a quiet moment of connection that doesn't remove the grief but makes it more bearable.

qa.q: How did continuing Papa's volunteering help Sudha?
qa.a: Reading to Mr Fernandes as Papa did kept a link to Papa and let Sudha share memories, making the loss feel less lonely.

qa.q: How might Mr Fernandes feel when Sudha reads to him?
qa.a: Mr Fernandes likely feels touched and comforted, sharing memories of Papa and holding Sudha's hand during the tears.

grounding: It shows an adult who finds comfort after losing a father through ritual and helping others, which makes the grief more bearable though it remains.

passage:
Gopika: are you coming to the gurdwara tomorrow
Ganga: i don't know. i don't feel like seeing people
Gopika: i get it. i didn't either, after Nani
Gopika: but the langar seva helped me more than anything
Ganga: how
Gopika: my hands were busy. rolling rotis next to aunties who knew her. they told stories about her i'd never heard
Gopika: i still cried in the car after. but it felt like she was part of something bigger, not just gone
Ganga: i miss her so much
Gopika: me too. every day
Ganga: ok. i'll come. can i stand next to you
Gopika: always
Ganga: thank you

qa.q: What seva did Gopika do after Nani died?
qa.a: Langar seva, rolling rotis next to aunties who knew her.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel after the langar seva?
qa.a: Gopika still cried afterwards but felt comforted, as if Nani was part of something bigger, not just gone.

qa.q: What might help Ganga through the next few days?
qa.a: Going to the gurdwara with Gopika and joining the seva could offer community, busy hands and shared memories of Nani.

qa.q: How is Ganga feeling about going?
qa.a: Ganga feels hesitant and heavy with grief, not wanting to see people, but willing to go if Gopika stands beside her.

grounding: It shows adults finding comfort after losing a grandmother through faith, community and service, which makes the grief more bearable.

passage: In the village near Kumbakonam, Leela's mother had taught at the small primary school for thirty years. After she died in the monsoon, Leela came home from Chennai for the rituals and couldn't bring herself to leave. Every morning, the house was too still. Her friend Arohi, a teacher at the same school, asked if she'd help with the reading hour, just for a week. Leela hesitated, then went. The children sat on the mat under the neem tree, as they had with her mother. One small girl said, "Your amma used to do the voices." Leela did the voices. Her throat tightened, but she kept going. In the evening, she lit the lamp at her mother's photo and told her about the children. The grief was still there, heavy. But it had somewhere to sit now.

qa.q: How long had Leela's mother taught at the school?
qa.a: Thirty years.

qa.q: How did Leela feel doing the voices at reading hour?
qa.a: Her throat tightened with grief, but she felt a meaningful connection to her mother in carrying on something she did.

qa.q: Why might the reading hour help Leela bear the loss?
qa.a: Helping the children and continuing her mother's work gave the grief meaning and a place to rest, even though it didn't remove it.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel watching Leela with the children?
qa.a: Arohi likely feels tender and hopeful, glad she found a gentle way to support her friend.

grounding: It shows an adult who, after losing her mother, finds comfort in ritual, community and helping others, making the grief more bearable.

subtype: Recognising the limit and asking for help [Response]
passage:
March, a Monday. Yash had stopped answering calls. At the software company, he stared at the same screen for hours. At night he lay awake. He told his brother Suraj on the phone, "I'm fine, just busy."

April, a Saturday. Suraj visited and found the flat full of unopened food boxes and Yash thinner. That evening Yash sat down on the floor and said, quietly, "I'm not okay. I don't think I can handle this by myself." It was the first time he'd said it aloud. Suraj sat beside him. "Thank you for telling me. Let's call Mummy and Papa together. And find someone to talk to." They called their parents that night. Suraj helped him book an appointment with a psychologist.

May, a Wednesday. After his third session, Yash cooked dinner for the first time in weeks. "Asking was the hardest part," he told Suraj on the phone.

qa.q: What did Suraj find in Yash's flat?
qa.a: It was full of unopened food boxes.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when he finally said he wasn't okay?
qa.a: He felt low and overwhelmed, and saying it aloud for the first time took courage, though it brought some relief.

qa.q: Which steps did Suraj and Yash take, and why were they wise?
qa.a: They told their parents that night and booked a psychologist, bringing in family and a qualified professional instead of struggling alone.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when Yash said he couldn't handle it alone?
qa.a: Suraj probably felt worried but grateful that Yash finally trusted him enough to say it.

grounding: It shows an adult who realises he is not coping, tells his family and seeks a qualified professional, over several weeks.

subtype: Recognising the limit and asking for help [Response]
passage: Hemant, you look like you're carrying too much. Let me tell you about the year I nearly didn't manage. I was twenty-five, a young woman nursing in Kochi, working double shifts. I stopped sleeping. I cried in the supply cupboard between patients. I kept telling myself I was strong enough. Then one morning I forgot a patient's medicine time, which I never forget. I sat in the car park and thought, I'm not coping. That was the turning point. I called my mother first. She came on the next bus. Then I asked the hospital to connect me with a counsellor. It felt like admitting defeat. It wasn't. It was the wisest thing I did that year. Elizabeth learned then that reaching out is a skill, like any other. So, Hemant, who will you tell?

qa.q: What did young Elizabeth forget one morning?
qa.a: A patient's medicine time.

qa.q: How did young Elizabeth feel when she admitted she wasn't coping?
qa.a: She felt that asking for help was like admitting defeat, but it also brought relief once she took action.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the difference?
qa.a: When she recognised she wasn't coping after the medicine mistake and chose to call her mother and ask for a counsellor instead of pushing on alone.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's mother have felt taking the next bus?
qa.a: Her mother likely felt worried and protective, glad her daughter called.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how she recognised she was not coping, told family and sought a counsellor, seeing asking for help as good judgement.

passage: The monsoon had flooded the ground floor of their Mumbai building, the lift was broken, and Karthik had been working from home for weeks with a newborn who barely slept. He stopped eating properly. He snapped at everyone, then felt awful. One night, after the baby's crying finally stopped at three, he sat in the dark kitchen and realised he couldn't remember the last time he'd felt anything but tired and numb. When his wife Shalini came in, he said, "I'm not coping. I think I need help. Real help." She sat down and held his hand. "Okay. We'll get it." The next morning, they called his parents, who offered to come and stay for a week. Then Shalini found the number of a counsellor their doctor had recommended, and Karthik booked a session for Friday, water still ankle-deep in the lobby.

qa.q: What was broken in their building?
qa.a: The lift.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he sat in the dark kitchen?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and numb, realising he couldn't remember feeling anything but tired, which told him he wasn't coping.

qa.q: Why was Karthik's choice to ask for help wise?
qa.a: He recognised his limit and involved his wife, his parents and a counsellor, which is good judgement rather than weakness.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when Karthik says he needs help?
qa.a: Shalini may feel worried but relieved and supportive, glad he told her so they can face it together.

grounding: It shows an adult who realises he is not coping, tells his family and seeks a qualified professional.
